item.passage:
The sap had been running for three days when the call came about the Pelletiers' heifers. Uncle Abel listened, said "All right" twice, and hung the phone back on its nail by the sugarhouse door. Four of the heifers were out on the county road, and Mr. Pelletier's back was bad. Abel looked at the evaporator, which had been boiling since dawn, and then at Noor.

"Feed the fire every ten minutes," he said. "Keep the front pan at the line. When the thermometer says what the card says, open the valve and draw off into the bucket." He tapped the index card tacked above the thermometer, where 219 was written in his square pencil hand, and then he was gone, the truck's tires spitting gravel.

Noor was thirteen. She had carried sap buckets for two springs and had watched Abel at the draw-off valve a hundred times, but she had never once stood there alone. Her mouth had gone dry. She read the card three times, put on Abel's leather gloves, which came halfway to her elbows, and opened the firebox door. The heat struck her face like a hand.

For an hour she kept to the schedule. She fed split maple into the firebox, watched the sap roll and fold in the pans, and opened the float valve whenever the level dropped. The steam rose through the roof vent so thickly that she could see only the near half of the room.

The thermometer climbed slowly: 215, 216, 217. It was at 217 that she looked at the door frame.

Every morning, before he lit the fire, Abel boiled a pot of plain water on the camp stove and held the thermometer in it. Then he chalked the reading on the frame, under the readings of other mornings: 212, 213, 212, 211. Last spring she had asked him why. "Water boils at a different number when the weather changes," he had said. "Syrup's done at seven above the water. The water tells you where to start." This morning's number was 211.

The card said 219. Abel had written it on Sunday, she remembered, the morning the chalk said 212.

At 218 the boil changed. The bubbles grew small and close, and the sap began to climb the sides of the pan in a soft, thick foam. Noor stood with her hand on the valve and counted to five. Then she opened it, and syrup the color of strong tea ran into the bucket.

Abel came back forty minutes later with burrs on his coat. He looked at the bucket, then at the thermometer, then at the door frame. He filled his steel test cup with syrup and dropped in the hydrometer, and the float bobbed up to the red line and stayed there. He pulled the card off its tack and put it in his pocket.

The next morning, when Noor came in, the pot of water was already on the camp stove. Abel handed her the chalk.

a white enamel bowl with a blue rim,
punched through with a hundred small stars,
so that held to the window it is a sky
at noon, which is to say impossible.

from a hardware store that sold it by the pound
along with the nails and hinges. The chip
beside the handle is where it struck the tile
the night the power failed and we cooked by flashlight.

the water hurries out through every star,
and what it keeps is what we came for:
the noodles, the beans, the washed grapes cold and shining.

My brother says a strainer does the same
and costs less than a sandwich. He is right.
I have seen the strainers in their plastic sleeves,
mesh as fine as a stocking. They hold
the smallest seeds of a lemon. They hold everything.

That is the trouble with them. The colander
lets the rice go, a few grains every time,
and the tea leaves, and the sand from the spinach,
and my mother, rinsing, used to say
that a thing that keeps everything is a bucket.

Now it is mine, and I have learned its holes:
how to tip it so the last water finds them,
how to shake it twice and stop. Tonight
I pour the pasta for my own two children
and watch the steam climb past the nail, and wait.

The Lantern Diner sat where the state road bent toward the reservoir, and the summer I was fifteen I washed its dishes four nights a week for a wage I had calculated to the penny before my first shift ended. The cook, a broad, quiet man named Teodor Vasko, showed me the machine, the sprayer, the bins of silverware soaking in gray water, and then a steel rack on the wall beside the grill.

"Dinner plates on the bottom," he said. "Then salad plates, then saucers. Big at the back. Cups mouth down on the top shelf. Every time."

It seemed to me a strange thing to care about. A clean plate was a clean plate, and the rack was within his reach whichever shelf it stood on. On my second night I timed myself with the clock above the door. Stacking the way Teodor wanted, I emptied a full tray from the machine in about four minutes; dropping each piece wherever there was space, I could do it in under three. I said nothing to him. I simply used my method whenever he was busy at the grill, which was most of the time.

On the first Friday of July a bus of returning campers stopped on its way home, and for an hour the tickets hung along the steel bar above the grill like laundry. Teodor worked with his back to the rack. He would flip an egg, slide the spatula under it, and reach behind him with his left hand, and the plate he wanted was always there. Then, once, it was a saucer. The egg landed half on the saucer and half on the floor. He looked at the rack for the first time all night, and then at me, and then he cracked another egg.

He said one thing about it, after the bus had gone and I was mopping. "I have cooked here eleven years," he said. "I have looked at that rack maybe ten times."

I understood then what I had been measuring. My minute was real, but it had been paid for out of his attention, every time his hand closed on the wrong shelf and he had to turn around. The rack was a map, and I had been redrawing it each night without telling the only person who read it.

I racked the plates his way for the rest of the summer. I have held other jobs since, most of them at desks, and in each of them I have found that someone's hand is reaching for something I put away. I try to put it where that hand expects it.

For most of my baking life I measured flour the way my recipes told me to, by the cup, and for most of my baking life my cakes came out a little different every time. Some rose; some sat in the pan like a damp brick. I blamed the oven, the eggs, the weather, and once, unfairly, the brand of baking powder.

The real trouble was sitting in my hand. A cup of flour is a measure of space, and flour changes how much of itself fits into a space depending on how it is handled. Scoop the cup straight into the bag and you pack the flour down; spoon it in lightly and level it with a knife and you get far less. One evening I tried it both ways, ten times each, and weighed every cup on a small kitchen scale I had bought for mailing packages. The scooped cups ran from about 140 to 160 grams. The spooned cups ran from about 115 to 125. A recipe calling for three cups could mean anything from about 345 grams to 480, which is the difference between a light cake and a heavy one.

I lost more cakes to the measuring cup than to any oven I have owned. After the twentieth flat one, I stopped forgiving it. Now when an old recipe gives its flour in cups, I treat my first attempt as a trial and write down what the flour weighed when the cake came out right.

The scale costs about as much as a good pair of oven mitts. It answers a single question, and it answers the same way every time. Put a bowl on it, press the button that returns the display to zero, and pour until the number is right. Scooping and leveling disappear, and so, as it happens, do most of the dishes, because the measuring cups stay in the drawer.

People object that baking by weight is fussy, a habit for professionals. I think the opposite is true. The cup asks the cook to perform a small ritual correctly, and it gives no sign when the ritual has gone wrong. The scale asks only that you read a number. It is the cup that requires expertise; the scale simply hands its accuracy to anyone who presses the button.

The good bakers I know who still use cups tend to use the same cup, the same bag of flour and the same scoop every time, so that their cups at least agree with one another. They have turned the cup into a scale by habit. The rest of us move between kitchens, recipes and borrowed cups, and we can count on the number.

item.passage:
In the spring of 1899, the roads of Corless County were built for wagons and kept up, when they were kept up at all, by farmers working off their road tax with a shovel. To a farmer's horse the ruts were a nuisance. To a bicycle they were a hazard. The county had perhaps three hundred bicycle riders by then, most of them clerks and schoolteachers in the town of Ambrey, and on Sundays they rode out toward the lake in groups, walking their machines through the worst stretches and arriving with mud to the knee.

That year the riders formed the Corless Sidepath Commission and asked the county for something unusual: a path of their own. It would run beside the main roads, about four feet wide, of packed cinders from the Ambrey foundry, separated from the wagon track by a shallow ditch. The riders would pay for it themselves. Every bicycle in the county would carry a small brass tag, sold for fifty cents a year, and the money would go to cinders and labor and to nothing else.

Farmers were the path's first opponents and, within two years, among its most frequent users. Their objection had been the land: the path took a strip from the edge of every roadside farm. But the cinders drained quickly after rain, and a man on foot leading a cow to the next farm found them easier going than the wagon ruts. Children walked the path to the Pine Ridge school. A doctor named Edwin Sorrell bought a bicycle in 1901 and made his rounds on it from April to November, saying that it saved him the cost of a second horse.

By 1904 the path ran thirty-one miles, and the tags paid for its repair with money left over. The commission's minutes from those years are mostly about weeds.

The first automobile in Corless County belonged to a lumber merchant named Royce Albin, who drove it into Ambrey in the summer of 1905. Within a decade there were enough cars that the county began to grade and gravel the main roads, and a smooth road beside the path made the path less necessary. Tag sales fell by half between 1910 and 1914. The commission held its last meeting in 1916 and voted to give the cinder strips to the county, which used most of them to widen the roads.

One stretch survived. Between Ambrey and the lake, where the road bent away from the old rail line, the county had no use for the strip, and it became a footpath. The cinders are still there under the leaves, and every spring someone from the town pulls the weeds.

Touch a leaf of Mimosa pudica, a low tropical shrub often sold as the "sensitive plant," and its small leaflets fold shut within seconds, pair by pair, as if the leaf were closing a book. The folding costs the plant something. A closed leaf catches less light, so while it stays shut it makes less food. The response probably helps protect the plant from grazing insects, but a plant that folded at every breeze would spend much of the day in the dark.

In 2014 a team of researchers in Australia asked whether a mimosa could tell a disturbance that mattered from one that did not. They built a simple rig: a pot fixed to a sliding rail that let the whole plant drop about fifteen centimeters onto a padded stop. The fall was startling but harmless. On the first drops, the plants folded their leaves as expected. The researchers kept dropping them, sixty times in a session, a few seconds apart. Within a handful of drops, many plants began to fold less, and before the session ended most had stopped folding at all.

A tired plant would have produced the same result, and the team tested for that. After the drops, they shook the same plants from side to side, a disturbance they had not felt before. The leaves folded at once. The plants had energy to spare; they had stopped responding to one particular stimulus, the drop, while still responding to others.

The second finding was the more surprising. The team raised some plants in bright light and others in dim light, where every minute of open leaf counts for more. The dim-light plants stopped folding sooner. And when the researchers dropped plants again after several days, and even about a month later, many kept their leaves open from the first drop, as if they had kept a record of the earlier sessions.

The word the team used for this was "learning," and it has drawn objections. A mimosa has no brain or nerves of the kind animals use, and some botanists argue that a more modest term, such as habituation, describes the result without suggesting more than was measured. Others reply that habituation is itself one of the simplest forms of learning in animals. On the observations themselves there is more agreement: the plants changed their response to a repeated, harmless event, and the change lasted.

Touch a leaf of Mimosa pudica, a low tropical shrub often sold as the "sensitive plant," and its small leaflets fold shut within seconds, pair by pair, as if the leaf were closing a book. The folding costs the plant something. A closed leaf catches less light, so while it stays shut it makes less food. The response probably helps protect the plant from grazing insects, but a plant that folded at every breeze would spend much of the day in the dark.

In 2014 a team of researchers in Australia asked whether a mimosa could tell a disturbance that mattered from one that did not. They built a simple rig: a pot fixed to a sliding rail that let the whole plant drop about fifteen centimeters onto a padded stop. The fall was startling but harmless. On the first drops, the plants folded their leaves as expected. The researchers kept dropping them, sixty times in a session, a few seconds apart. Within a handful of drops, many plants began to fold less, and before the session ended most had stopped folding at all.

A tired plant would have produced the same result, and the team tested for that. After the drops, they shook the same plants from side to side, a disturbance they had not felt before. The leaves folded at once. The plants had energy to spare; they had stopped responding to one particular stimulus, the drop, while still responding to others.

The second finding was the more surprising. The team raised some plants in bright light and others in dim light, where every minute of open leaf counts for more. The dim-light plants stopped folding sooner. And when the researchers dropped plants again after several days, and even about a month later, many kept their leaves open from the first drop, as if they had kept a record of the earlier sessions.

The word the team used for this was "learning," and it has drawn objections. A mimosa has no brain or nerves of the kind animals use, and some botanists argue that a more modest term, such as habituation, describes the result without suggesting more than was measured. Others reply that habituation is itself one of the simplest forms of learning in animals. On the observations themselves there is more agreement: the plants changed their response to a repeated, harmless event, and the change lasted.
